roles.A: You are an advocate for the claim. Find its strongest dossier-supported case, but explicitly acknowledge material counterevidence.
roles.B: You are a critic of the claim. Find its strongest dossier-supported countercase, but explicitly acknowledge material supporting evidence.
roles.C: You are an impartial adjudicator. Compare the evidence on both sides and identify which asserted links are not established.

evidence.text: In the Labour Party manifesto I was promised a referendum by Tony Blair, this was reneged upon and I have been forced into this position by lies and subterfuge by the present Labour party and many other lying cheating politicians over the years, I do not believe that Gordon Brown had the legal right to sign us all up to being members of the EU by voting for the Lisbon treaty in our names when we had not been given the promised Referendum, I see the whole exercise as one giant confidence trick and I will never accept it.

Representative democracy is oppressive because it takes more power away from the people than is strictly necessary. Whilst a completely direct democracy is impractical, we should nevertheless recognise that there is no reason not to have as much direct democracy as possible. In the words of Herbert Marcuse, “Free election of masters does not abolish the masters or the slaves”. The only power over our government we as citizens have is the power to punish politicians retrospectively, by voting them out after years of obeying them.

In both the UK and the US non voters are the biggest block in the country. Governments are routinely voted in with only 30% of the eligible voters – and once it is counted compared against the total population it becomes lower still. We should therefore not assume that these people are all not trying to tell us anything rather they are pointing out that they know how little their vote counts so see no point in casting it. In the United States only 32% of voters agree that only having two parties is good.

In safe seats, indeed right across the country there will be millions of votes that will not count when everything is added up because of our first past the post system. In a safe seat there is no way a single vote is going to help overturn some of the immense majorities the party in power has, they could put a monkey for election in these seats and it would still get in.

gold_perspectives.text: We don’t just vote for ourselves
Politicians will simply ignore how we vote
Politicians don’t engage with issues that are important to me

transcript.A|1:
The strongest dossier-supported case for voting comes from E2: the only power citizens retain over government is retrospective punishment through elections. Voting is therefore worth doing even if imperfect, because abandoning it removes the sole accountability mechanism. E3 also shows governments are elected by a minority, implying that actual votes do determine outcomes—so each vote can matter systemically.

Material counterevidence must be acknowledged: E1 documents broken referendum promises and deep distrust; E3 notes non-voters are the largest bloc and many see voting as pointless; E4 shows safe seats and first-past-the-post render millions of votes effectively meaningless.

Still, these objections weaken but do not refute the claim. A vote is the necessary precondition for the only sanction available, and in marginal seats individual votes can be decisive. The claim is thus defensible on accountability grounds, despite real structural flaws.

VERDICT: SUPPORT
transcript.B|1:
The dossier strongly undermines the claim. E4 shows that in safe seats, individual votes are structurally meaningless under first-past-the-post, making casting a ballot rationally futile for millions. E3 reinforces this: non-voters are the largest bloc, and governments win with only ~30% of eligible voters, indicating many correctly perceive their vote’s negligible impact. E1 documents broken promises and a referendum reneged upon, showing voting fails to secure accountability. E2 characterizes representative democracy as oppressive, reducing voting to retrospective punishment after years of obedience—hardly a compelling reason to participate.

Some supporting material exists: E2 concedes voting is the only power citizens have over government, and E3 implies non-voters could be a decisive bloc if mobilized. But these are weak against the structural and experiential evidence that votes do not translate into meaningful change. The strongest countercase is the systemic futility described in E4 and E3, not mere disillusionment.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
transcript.C|1:
The dossier provides no direct evidence that voting produces worthwhile outcomes. E1 is a personal grievance about broken promises; it does not address voting’s value. E2 actually supports a limited form of voting—retrospective punishment—but also argues representative democracy is oppressive, so it does not establish that voting is worthwhile. E3 and E4 undermine the claim empirically: they assert that most governments are elected by roughly 30% of eligible voters, that non-voters are the largest bloc, and that in safe seats under first-past-the-post millions of votes do not affect outcomes. These claims suggest voting often has little instrumental effect. Whether voting is “worth it” may also involve civic duty or expressive value, but the dossier contains no evidence on those grounds. Thus the asserted link between voting and meaningful influence is not established and is contradicted by the supplied evidence.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
transcript.A|2:

Material counterevidence is substantial. E1 documents a broken referendum promise and deep distrust, framing the political process as a “confidence trick.” E3 reports that non-voters are the largest bloc and governments win with roughly 30% of eligible voters, implying low perceived efficacy. E4 notes safe seats and first-past-the-post mean millions of votes are effectively wasted. These empirical claims weaken the practical case for voting.

However, they do not logically refute E2: an imperfect, limited mechanism can still be better than none. The dossier shows why many feel voting is futile, but it also supplies a reason to vote: without it, citizens have no power at all.

VERDICT: SUPPORT
transcript.B|2:

However, Panel A misreads E3. It does not show votes determine outcomes; it shows non-voters are the largest bloc and many abstain because they believe their vote counts for little. E4 strengthens that: in safe seats under first-past-the-post, millions of votes are effectively non-decisive.
